name: Training Data and Opt-Outs
title: Training Data and Opt-Outs
answer: Training data and opt-outs concern the datasets used to teach generative image, video, and audio models, and the mechanisms by which artists and rights holders can ask for their work to be excluded. It covers how data is collected, filtered, and documented, and what an opt-out actually means in practice. The page sits within rights and provenance because the choice of training inputs shapes both legal exposure and the stylistic outputs of a model. It also addresses the difference between opting out of future training and removing work already learned by a model.

sections.body: Training data and opt-outs concern the datasets used to teach generative image, video, and audio models, and the mechanisms by which artists and rights holders can ask for their work to be excluded. It covers how data is collected, filtered, and documented, and what an opt-out actually means in practice. The page sits within rights and provenance because the choice of training inputs shapes both legal exposure and the stylistic outputs of a model. It also addresses the difference between opting out of future training and removing work already learned by a model.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Training data for art models is typically assembled from large web crawls, image hosting sites, stock libraries, and public datasets. Opt-out infrastructure includes per-site robots.txt directives, centralized do-not-train registries, and platform-specific forms that let creators flag their work. These signals must then be matched against the data pipeline before training begins, which requires stable identifiers and periodic re-crawls. In practice, the infrastructure is fragmented, and a single opt-out rarely propagates across all datasets or model trainers.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work of building training sets is often done by automated scraping, deduplication, and pairing images or clips with text descriptions. Opt-out processing is a filtering step: a crawler checks a URL or content hash against an exclusion list and drops matching items. Some teams also use provenance metadata, such as copyright notices or watermarks, to detect and remove opted-out material. The method is imperfect because models may still learn from near-duplicates, cropped versions, or descriptions that mention the work without including the image itself.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on whether training on copyrighted work without permission is fair use, and whether an opt-out creates a binding obligation. In the 92 active intellectual property lawsuits this atlas tracks, courts are testing whether scraping, memorization, and output similarity cross legal lines. Opt-out systems are often voluntary, so a creator who opts out has no guarantee that every trainer will honor the request. Contracts, terms of service, and emerging transparency rules are beginning to turn some opt-outs into enforceable conditions rather than polite signals.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Opt-outs are moving from ad hoc lists toward machine-readable standards that can be checked automatically during data collection. The likely direction is a combination of persistent content credentials, registry-based exclusion, and technical unlearning methods that try to reduce the influence of removed work after training. As more jurisdictions require training data disclosure, opt-out records may become part of a model's provenance file. The unresolved question is whether retroactive opt-outs can ever fully undo what a model has already absorbed.
